---
title: "Storage, Distribution, and Interop"
---

## Principle

Cellerator owns biological execution semantics.

Adjacent systems move, persist, expose, or adapt Cellerator artifacts without redefining those semantics.

```text
Baseplane
    sequence-specialized computation

Cellerator
    domains, structures, geometry, planning, kernels, state

CellShard
    persistence, sharding, transport, staging, publication

CelleraTorch
    framework adaptation
```

## CellShard boundary

CellShard owns data handling when biological computation is too large or too distributed to treat as one local object.

Its responsibilities include:

- canonical dataset persistence;
- source ingest;
- dataset and partition identity;
- sharded storage;
- execution-envelope publication;
- checksums and versioning;
- active generation selection;
- cache and fetch;
- host and device staging;
- delivery to active workers;
- distributed storage-oriented partition artifacts;
- cold metadata retrieval;
- archive maintenance.

Cellerator owns:

- biological domains and relations;
- semantic geometry;
- row and feature order;
- module and hierarchy semantics;
- projection meaning;
- operation semantics;
- planner and autotuner;
- kernels;
- execution order;
- numerical state.

## Current persistence seam

The current CP-BP persistence path uses:

- a Cellerator-owned CPK1 image;
- a CellShard-owned execution envelope;
- explicit dataset, partition, generation, feature-axis, and payload compatibility;
- contiguous upload;
- Cellerator-side rebinding;
- direct native execution.

This ownership seam is sound.

The inner image should evolve into a sectioned execution image. The outer CellShard envelope may remain generic and opaque.

## Canonical storage versus execution images

Canonical storage and execution images serve different purposes.

### Canonical storage

Optimized for:

- durability;
- complete identity;
- interoperability;
- reconstruction;
- append or generation management;
- architecture independence.

### Execution image

Optimized for:

- direct accelerator ingest;
- stable order;
- physical projection;
- compact metadata;
- pointer rebinding;
- repeated execution;
- architecture or workload specialization.

An execution image is derived and replaceable. It is not the only source of biological truth.

## Persistence contract

A CellShard execution envelope should validate:

- envelope schema;
- payload kind and schema;
- dataset identity;
- partition identity;
- generation;
- source domain identities;
- dimensions;
- byte bounds;
- checksum;
- target compatibility metadata.

Cellerator validates:

- execution-image sections;
- domain and order identity;
- geometry;
- structure epoch;
- canonical recovery maps;
- projection consistency;
- index bounds;
- masks;
- value layout;
- kernel compatibility.

CellShard must not parse or reinterpret projection-specific tile semantics.

## Storage of structure and values

Structure and values have different change frequencies.

CellShard should be able to persist:

- structure image once;
- one or more value planes;
- value-generation metadata;
- optional alternate precision planes;
- optional projection-specific reordered values;
- deltas or checkpoints when appropriate.

It should not require rebuilding or duplicating the structure for every value generation.

## Projection persistence policy

Persist a physical projection when:

- construction is expensive;
- reuse is high;
- its target device class is known;
- storage expansion is acceptable;
- it remains valid for the structure epoch.

Build lazily when:

- use is uncertain;
- deployment device is unknown;
- construction is cheap;
- the operation is rare.

Discard or rebuild when:

- structure changes;
- kernel ABI changes;
- device performance class changes materially;
- persistent memory cost exceeds amortized benefit.

## Distribution

CellShard may deliver:

- a complete structure image;
- one partition;
- one projection section;
- one value plane;
- boundary-edge data;
- sequence chunks and halos;
- communication schedules;
- prepared runtime artifacts that Cellerator validates.

The transport unit need not equal the biological partition or the kernel tile.

Keep these concepts separate:

```text
biological partition
    execution partition
        storage extent
            transport unit
```

## Multi-GPU partitioning

Cellerator chooses computation-aware partitions. CellShard stores and routes them.

Possible Cellerator partition axes include:

- cell or batch;
- feature or gene;
- biological module;
- regulatory program;
- sequence coordinate;
- hybrid nested partition.

CellPack may optimize a cut term. CellShard persists the resulting ownership and boundary sections.

## Communication in execution order

A distributed prepared program should communicate data in the order required by the destination consumer.

```text
local execution-order values
    ↓ pack boundary values
peer, NCCL, or network transfer
    ↓
destination execution-order input
```

Canonical order should not be inserted merely because transport is occurring.

## Replication versus communication

Small, frequently used structures or modules may be replicated.

Large, infrequently crossed relations may be partitioned.

The planner should compare:

\[
C_{\text{replicate}}
=
C_{\text{extra memory}}
+
C_{\text{update replication}}
\]

against:

\[
C_{\text{communicate}}
=
f_{\text{use}}
\cdot
C_{\text{transfer}}
+
C_{\text{sync}}
\]

CellShard executes the chosen delivery plan. Cellerator decides it.

## Sequence distribution

Baseplane sequence domains may be sharded by coordinate with halos.

CellShard may store and deliver:

- packed sequence chunks;
- validity;
- coordinate identity;
- owned range;
- halo;
- prepared sequence artifacts;
- static sequence-derived relations.

Cellerator and Baseplane define event ownership and cross-boundary semantics.

## CelleraTorch

CelleraTorch is an explicit adapter.

It may create:

- zero-copy Torch views when memory, dtype, shape, stride, order, and lifetime permit;
- custom operators that invoke prepared Cellerator operations;
- framework modules that own only framework-facing configuration;
- deliberate conversion when Torch requires a different representation.

It must not:

- make Torch own canonical Cellerator parameter allocation by default;
- hide per-step sparse conversion;
- rebuild structure in every forward;
- discard biological domain and order identity;
- define a competing planner;
- duplicate native kernels.

## Parameter exposure

Native parameters should remain:

- pointer-stable;
- explicitly shaped and strided;
- associated with domain and order identity;
- associated with structure and value generation;
- writable or read-only by contract;
- distinguishable from optimizer state.

CelleraTorch may expose views over that storage.

When a zero-copy view is impossible, conversion cost must be explicit and benchmarked at the intended reuse.

## Python and workflow adapters

High-level APIs may orchestrate:

- dataset selection;
- preparation;
- execution;
- result publication;
- metrics.

They must not perform hidden CPU transforms over matrices that the native core should process.

A Python convenience layer does not change ownership:

- Cellerator owns numerical semantics;
- CellShard owns persistence;
- Baseplane owns sequence primitives;
- CelleraTorch owns Torch adaptation.

## Interop identity

Every adapter must preserve or translate:

- domain identity;
- order;
- partition;
- structure epoch;
- value generation;
- dtype;
- shape and stride;
- device;
- ownership and lifetime.

An adapter that returns only pointer and dimensions is incomplete for biological data.

## Prohibited boundary patterns

Do not use:

```text
Baseplane → host table → Cellerator
Cellerator → canonical CSR → CellShard → same-GPU Cellerator
Cellerator → Torch sparse conversion → native Cellerator
execution order → canonical order → transport → execution order
```

unless the complete measured path proves that the boundary wins.

## Future compiled programs

A future compiled Cellerator program may package:

- domain and relation identity;
- semantic geometry;
- projection requirements;
- prepared-plan metadata;
- kernel build compatibility;
- graph and communication schedule.

Such a format must not drive current ABI design prematurely.

The immediate priority is a stable structure, value, order, and projection model.

## Boundary checklist

Before adding cross-repository code, verify:

- Which repository owns the semantics?
- Which repository owns the bytes?
- Which repository chooses the layout?
- Which repository chooses the kernel?
- Is identity preserved?
- Is a copy necessary?
- Can the producer emit the consumer's order?
- Can the result remain device-resident?
- Is the artifact canonical or derived?
- Does a generation or structure epoch invalidate it?
- Is the conversion included in the planner?
- Will the boundary work for multi-GPU execution?

The correct boundary is the one that moves the fewest bytes while leaving ownership unambiguous.

## CE-GEO persistence and interop outcome

CSG1 remains portable and pointer-free; CPE2 may embed the compatible physical
projection for delivery; CPK1 compatibility bytes remain frozen. CellShard
transports these opaque artifacts and retains storage, sharding, staging, and
distribution ownership. Cellerator owns validation, projection meaning,
execution order, and numerical use after acquisition. The final baseline and
acceptance campaigns replayed CPK1/CPE2 compatibility without rewriting stored
history or transferring file ownership into the compute core.
